content.text: While the researchers run, I'll draw the current system on the canvas.

Base directory for this skill: /home/agus/workspace/asermax/claude-plugins/mahou/skills/canvas

Load mahou:basics first. Then read `.mahou/canvas.md` if present.

# Canvas

## Documents

A canvas is one document, `<name>.tldr.json`, in a folder a loading skill names along with the name. When the user types the skill, the folder is `canvas/` in the change's scratch folder and the document is named after what it draws. A folder can hold several documents.

- `<name>.tldr.json` is the document. The server holds it while the canvas runs and saves every edit to it, from any tab. Its `canvasVersion` names its format.
- `<name>.svg` is its export, next to it.
- `mockups/` holds the mockups every document in the folder can draw, one `<kind>.tsx` file each. A mockup is the content of the canvas's custom `mock` shape, for anything the stock tldraw shapes do not draw, such as a screen. Its file exports `mockup`, a `MockDefinition<Props>` from `@canvas/MockShape`: its natural width, its default props and a function that renders them. A `mock` shape's `data` is merged over the defaults, so a shape passes only what differs, such as `{ kind: 'login', data: { state: 'error' } }`. A `mock` shape draws its kind at the natural width and scales the drawing to the shape's size, so one mockup renders at any shape size. Every open tab reloads when a file in `mockups/` is added or changed.

## Running it

`scripts/canvas.sh` runs the app over one document. Pass it the document's path:

- `start` installs the app on first run, starts the server detached and prints the URL to give the user. One server runs at a time: starting another document stops the server for the first, whose document is already on disk. It refuses a document saved in an older format and names the `migrate` command.
- `watch` prints one line per "Send to Claude" click.
- `export` writes `<name>.svg`.
- `texts` prints every canvas text and arrow label, one per line.
- `migrate` brings an older document to the current format, keeping the original as `<name>.tldr.json.bak`. Run it with the server stopped. When it warns that a mockup received a variant string, rewrite that mockup to read its props from `data`.
- `stop` stops the server.

Build and edit the canvas from scripts run with `agent-browser` in your own tab, opened once on `<URL>?user=Claude` and kept open, so the user sees your cursor under that name. Every tab edits the same document live: your changes appear in the user's tab as you make them, and theirs in yours. The page exposes `window.editor`, `window.tldraw` with `createShapeId` and `toRichText`, and `window.canvas` with `notes()` and `step(at, change, pause?)`.

Draw in steps the user can follow. A script's changes reach the other tabs together, so a script that draws everything at once shows the user only the finished result. Run each element as an awaited `canvas.step`: it moves your cursor to `at` (a shape id or a page point, or `null` to stay), applies `change`, and waits `pause` milliseconds, 500 by default. One step per shape, arrow or move, in the order a person would draw them: follow the flow the drawing explains, and join each element to what it connects to as soon as both are on the canvas, so the drawing grows as one connected piece and never as all the boxes first and all the arrows last.

- An area goes first, before what it holds.
- After the first element, each new element is followed right away by the arrow that joins it to what is already drawn, then by that arrow's label if it has one.
- A note goes right after the element it describes, and its arrow right after the note.

Check every change with a screenshot, saved under a new file name each time, since reading a path you read before can show the earlier image.

## Mockups

Mockups import the shared pieces from `@canvas/kit`: `theme`, with the ink, paper, colours, hand font and a sketched border, and `Browser`, a browser window around a screen. Three kinds are built in: `cylinder`, whose data is `{ title, caption }`; `area`, a rounded dashed region whose data is `{ label }`, for grouping the shapes inside a part, used instead of a frame and sent to the back; and `blank-screen`.

Keep them low fidelity: the hand font, sketched borders, and grey bars for text that does not matter.

When the screen has a prototype, copy the mockup from it: the same parts, the same states and the same copy, translated into the language the canvas is written in. A state that is its own view in the prototype is its own mockup on the canvas.

## Drawing

- **Notes are free text.** A short sentence with an arrow to the spot it describes. Never a sticky note, since sticky notes are the user's messages.
- **Arrows point at an element's centre**, so they follow when the element moves. An arrow points at a specific spot only when it means that spot: a button, an option, a row.
- Text is black, arrow labels included.
- **Box the parts of one thing with an `area`, never a frame.** When several separate shapes are parts of the same thing, such as the variants of one part or the screens of one sequence, draw a `mock` shape of kind `area` around them. Send it to the back. Shapes that only sit near each other get no area.
- **Group what moves together.** Each element, or each set of elements that belong together, is one tldraw group with its title, made with `editor.groupShapes`. Group no further than the smallest set that is one cohesive thing. Elements joined by arrows can share a group, such as the steps of one flow. An element that stands on its own gets its own group, even when an arrow joins it to another element. Arrows between two groups stay outside both, so they stay attached at each end when either group moves.

## Working with the user

- **Your tab holds the current state.** Read what you change from `window.editor` right before changing it, since the user may have moved it. Once the user has edited the canvas, never rebuild it; change only the shapes the change touches.
- **Never reuse a deleted shape's id.** Sync sends a deleted shape recreated under its id as an update to the old record, so a new shape of another type under that id fails validation in every open tab.
- **A sticky note on the canvas is a message from the user.** When you give the user the URL, tell them to put a sticky note on the shape they want changed, or to draw an arrow from the note to it. `window.canvas.notes()` returns each note with its targets: the shapes an arrow joins it to, else the shapes it sits on, smallest first. Act on each note, and once it is handled, delete it together with its `arrows` and tell the user.
- **"Send to Claude" notifies that a batch of edits is ready.** The document is already saved. Keep a watch on `canvas.sh watch` while the canvas is open; each line is a click. Do not react to the user's edits between clicks. When the watch times out, start it again.

## Export

1. **Unslop the texts.** Collect the output of `canvas.sh texts` and the explanatory texts written inside the mockups the document uses into a file in the change's scratch folder, and run superpowers:unslop over it. When that skill is not installed, say so and continue. Apply the findings that survive verification to the canvas and the mockups.
2. **Export.** Run `canvas.sh export`. The loading skill places the SVG where it needs the image.

## What this skill is not

It does not commit.

{"pane_id":"w3W:p9","label":"research: api runtime on cloudflare","agent":"research-api-runtime-on-cloudfla","status":"done","message":"# Report: where nagara's API can run on Cloudflare (as of 2026-10-04)

I ran no trials. Every claim below comes from documentation, changelogs or news pages, and each is tagged **(docs)**, **(changelog)** or **(news)**. Pyodide 314.0.7 package facts come from its own package list **(docs)**.

## 1. Python Workers (Pyodide) running FastAPI
Docs: https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/languages/python/

- **R1.**
  - FastAPI runs through a built-in ASGI connector (`workers.asgi`) **(docs: .../python/packages/fastapi/)**.
  - GA announced 2026-09-21, two years after the preview **(blog.cloudflare.com/python-workers-ga, InfoQ)**.
  - ASGI/WSGI support landed 2026-09-02, and Python 3.14 became the default for compatibility date 2026-09-08 and later, on Pyodide 314.0.6 **(changelog)**.
  - Your app is pinned to Python 3.12. An older compatibility date is the likely route to an older Python, but I did not verify that.
- **R2.**
  - Supported: pure-Python wheels, PyEmscripten wheels, and packages bundled in Pyodide **(docs)**.
  - Pyodide 314.0.7 ships Pillow 12.2.0, httpx 0.28.1, SQLAlchemy 2.0.48, pydantic 2.12.5, aiohttp 3.13.5 and cffi **(docs)**.
  - Not in that list: cairosvg, boto3, grpcio **(docs)**.
  - cairosvg needs libcairo, which is native. I found no PyEmscripten wheel for it, but did not search PyPI.
  - The `modal` client depends on grpcio, so it is not in Pyodide. I found no evidence it can run on Workers.
  - Cloudflare's docs list no vendored packages for google-genai or firecrawl-py. Both are pure Python, but their dependency trees were not checked.
  - boto3 is pure Python, but I did not test it. A package missing from Pyodide can still install if all its wheels are pure or PyEmscripten.
  - HTTP clients are routed through JS `fetch` **(news: InfoQ)**.
  - SQLAlchemy async over asyncpg to Postgres would go through Hyperdrive. Hyperdrive support landed 2026-09-16 **(changelog via search result)**. asyncpg compatibility is not verified.
- **R3.** See cross-cutting section.
- **R4.**
  - `waitUntil` extends execution up to 30 s after the response **(docs: workers/platform/limits)**.
  - CPU time on Paid is 30 s by default and up to 5 min. Waiting on network I/O does not count toward CPU time.
  - Wall time has no hard limit while the client stays connected.
  - Queue consumers and Cron Triggers get 15 min of wall time per invocation.
  - Memory is 128 MB per isolate, including WASM allocations. The bundle limit is 64 MiB uncompressed (changed 2026-09-04).
  - GA coverage lists bindings to Queues, Workflows and Durable Objects from Python **(news/blog)**. Alarm usage from Python was not verified.
  - A Python Workflow or Queue consumer could run the Firecrawl-then-POST step beyond 30 s. The Worker limits above apply.
- **R5.** D1, R2, Durable Objects, Queues, Workflows, Workers AI and Vectorize are available as bindings **(news/blog)**. Service bindings from Python were not explicitly confirmed. The docs say "KV, D1, Durable Objects, Workers AI, R2, and other services through bindings" **(docs)**.
- **R6.**
  - Cold start uses a WASM memory snapshot taken at deploy time **(docs: how-python-workers-work)**.
  - One benchmark measured about 1.027 s startup. Cloudflare said it has since improved **(news: InfoQ)**. Treat this as an unconfirmed third-party figure.
  - Workers scale to zero by nature.
- **R7.** There is no process for running Alembic at deploy time. D1 migrations use `wrangler d1 migrations apply` with `.sql` files tracked in a `d1_migrations` table **(docs: d1/reference/migrations)**. SQLAlchemy/Alembic against D1 is not described in the docs.

## 2. Cloudflare Containers running the existing image
Docs: https://developers.cloudflare.com/containers/

- **R1.** The container runs uvicorn and FastAPI, so no ASGI adapter is involved. Containers and Sandboxes went GA on 2026-04-13 **(changelog)**. Workers Paid is required.
- **R2.** Any Linux image runs, including libcairo, grpcio, `modal`, Pillow, boto3 and the rest. I verified none of this by build. Docker Hub images and registries are supported **(changelog)**.
- **R4.**
  - Deferred work runs in the container process like it does today. The container lives while it is active. It sleeps after `sleepAfter`, which defaults to 10 min **(docs: architecture)**.
  - Platform shutdown sends SIGTERM, then SIGKILL after up to 15 min.
  - Worker-side tools (Queues, Workflows, DO alarms) sit in the fronting Worker, not in the container.
- **R5.**
  - Access to a container goes only through a Durable Object via `ctx.container` **(docs)**.
  - The container reaches bindings (R2, D1, KV, DOs) through outbound handlers. These are programmable egress proxies that run on the same machine as the container. The container makes plain HTTP calls to hostnames you map with `outboundByHost` **(docs: platform-details/outbound-traffic)**.
  - Service bindings are not named on that page. R2 over the S3 API from boto3 was not verified.
- **R6.**
  - Instance types **(docs: platform-details/limits)**:

    | Type | vCPU | Memory | Disk |
    |---|---|---|---|
    | lite | 1/16 | 256 MiB | 2 GB |
    | basic | 1/4 | 1 GiB | 4 GB |
    | standard-1 | 1/2 | 4 GiB | 8 GB |
    | standard-2 | 1 | 6 GiB | 12 GB |
    | standard-3 | 2 | 8 GiB | 16 GB |
    | standard-4 | 4 | 12 GiB | 20 GB |

  - Custom types are possible within 1–4 vCPU, up to 12 GiB memory and up to 20 GB disk, with a 3 GiB per vCPU minimum.
  - An image cannot exceed the instance disk. Image storage is 50 GB per account.
  - Cold starts are "often 1–3 s", depending on image size and startup code **(docs)**.
  - Disk is ephemeral and resets on sleep, unless snapshots are used.
  - Pricing is active-CPU **(changelog)**.
- **R7.** A container entrypoint or startup command can run `alembic upgrade head`. This is not documented as a deploy-time step. Postgres is not part of Containers. The database would be D1 or an external Postgres.

## 3. TypeScript Worker
Docs: https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/

- **R1.** Not applicable. Workers are GA. Hono-style frameworks would replace FastAPI. I did not research Hono.
- **R2.** Only npm packages. Of your dependencies, only httpx, boto3-style S3 access and the Gemini and Firecrawl SDKs would map to JS equivalents. I did not research those packages. The `modal` Python client has no JS equivalent in this research.
- **R4.** Same limits as in section 1. `waitUntil` allows 30 s. Queues, Workflows and Durable Object alarms are all available natively.
- **R5.** Native bindings to D1, R2, Durable Objects, and service bindings to the extraction Worker. Per your context, those are already in use.
- **R6.** Isolates start in milliseconds and scale to zero. I did not look up a figure for this.
- **R7.** D1 migrations through wrangler (see section 1).

## Cross-cutting facts

- **R3 — calling Modal over HTTP.**
  - Modal's docs show no public REST API for spawning a function and polling by call id.
  - Modal's documented HTTP route is a web endpoint you write: `@modal.fastapi_endpoint`, `@modal.asgi_app` and similar **(docs: modal.com/docs/guide/webhooks)**. Endpoints can be protected with proxy auth tokens (key and secret headers).
  - The documented job-queue pattern uses two endpoints **(docs: modal.com/docs/guide/job-queue)**.
    - `POST /submit` calls `fn.spawn.aio(data)` and returns `{"call_id": call.object_id}`.
    - `GET /result/{call_id}` calls `modal.FunctionCall.from_id(call_id).get.aio(timeout=0)`. It returns 202 while the job runs and 404 on `OutputExpiredError`. Results expire after 7 days.
  - A Pyodide or TypeScript caller would use plain `fetch` against those endpoints. That requires deploying two web endpoints on the Modal side, so the TTS service gains an HTTP surface.
  - Audio would still come back base64 in the JSON result, as it does today.
- **Workers and the existing extraction Worker.** Python Workers and TS Workers both sit in the same runtime as the extraction Worker, so they can reach D1, R2 and DOs through bindings. Containers reach them only via the outbound-handler path.
- **Python and Pyodide status.** The Python Workers stack is GA but young: the 64 MiB bundle limit changed on 2026-09-04, and the GA announcement is 13 days old.

## Not verified

- Whether cairosvg, grpcio, google-genai, firecrawl-py or boto3 install and run on Python Workers.
- Whether asyncpg works through Hyperdrive, and whether SQLAlchemy and Alembic work against D1.
- Service-binding usage and Durable Object alarms from Python.
- The Python-specific cold start and CPU/memory behaviour for a Pillow re-encode inside the 128 MB isolate.
- Whether a Python Workers compatibility date can pin Python 3.12.
- Whether a Container can call service bindings, and R2 through the S3 API.
- Modal's current client version and whether it works against gRPC from a non-CPython host.","ask":false}

{"pane_id":"w3W:pA","label":"research: cf data, storage, pricing","agent":"research-cf-data-storage-pricing","status":"done","message":"# Cloudflare vs Railway for nagara's API, database and bucket (as of 2026-10-04)

Each claim is tagged **[docs]** (fetched pricing/doc page), **[PyPI]** (registry metadata) or **[trial]**. I ran no trials, so nothing here is a verified fact in the sense of your brief.

## 1. D1
- Pricing [docs], https://developers.cloudflare.com/d1/platform/pricing/:
  - Free plan: 5M rows read/day, 100k rows written/day, 5 GB total storage.
  - Paid plan: 25 billion reads/month and 50M writes/month included, then $0.001 per million reads and $1.00 per million writes. 5 GB included, then $0.75/GB-month.
  - There are no egress or bandwidth charges.
- Limits [docs], https://developers.cloudflare.com/d1/platform/limits/:
  - Maximum database size is 10 GB on Paid and 500 MB on Free.
  - Maximum row, string or BLOB size is 2 MB.
  - Bound parameters per query are capped at 100.
  - Each Worker invocation gets 6 simultaneous D1 connections and 1,000 queries on Paid.
  - Each database is single-threaded.
- SQLite compatibility [docs]:
  - D1 runs on SQLite's query engine and includes the JSON extension, FTS5 and math functions.
  - `PRAGMA foreign_keys` and `defer_foreign_keys` are available, and `ON DELETE CASCADE` stays active even when enforcement is deferred.
  - `run()` returns `meta.changes` and `rows_written`, so a conditional `UPDATE ... WHERE` can be checked by its row count.
  - The docs I read say nothing on unique constraints beyond standard SQLite.
  - `batch()` runs its statements as one transaction that rolls back on failure.
- Access from a Python Worker [docs]: through the binding, as `self.env.DB.prepare(...).bind(...)` and `await self.env.DB.batch([...])`.
- Access from a Container or any non-Worker process [docs, PyPI]:
  - The only route documented is the REST API over HTTP.
  - I found no documented way to use a D1 binding from inside a Container.
  - A Worker in front of the Container acting as a proxy is an option; I did not verify it.
- SQLAlchemy [PyPI], https://pypi.org/project/sqlalchemy-cloudflare-d1/:
  - `sqlalchemy-cloudflare-d1` is at version 0.4.1, uploaded 2026-10-02, and needs Python 3.9 or newer.
  - Over HTTP it uses `cloudflare_d1://account_id:api_token@database_id`.
  - In a Python Worker it uses `create_engine_from_binding(self.env.DB)`.
  - `create_async_engine` works through an `[async]` extra, but the package's own description says async is unavailable inside Workers.
  - The repo's existing code uses async SQLAlchemy with asyncpg, so this is a driver change.
- Migrations [docs]: Prisma's own tutorial says "Prisma Migrate for D1 is currently in Early Access" and uses Wrangler for migrations and data. I did not verify Alembic against D1 or the Wrangler migration file format.
- Backups [docs], https://developers.cloudflare.com/d1/reference/time-travel/: Time Travel keeps 30 days on Paid and 7 days on Free at no extra cost. You restore with `wrangler d1 time-travel restore`, which overwrites data and returns a bookmark to undo it.
- Consistency [docs]:
  - Read replication is GA and adds no cost.
  - Without the Sessions API, all queries go to the primary.
  - With it you get sequential consistency: monotonic reads, monotonic writes and read-your-writes.

## 2. Hyperdrive
- Pricing [docs], https://developers.cloudflare.com/hyperdrive/platform/pricing/:
  - Hyperdrive is included in Workers plans. Paid has unlimited queries and Free has 100k/day.
  - It adds no data-transfer charges.
  - It provides connection pooling and query caching.
- It does not host a database. It sits in front of an external Postgres or MySQL you provide.
- The same page says Cloudflare's dashboard can provision PlanetScale Postgres or MySQL, billed on the Cloudflare invoice at PlanetScale's rates. I did not fetch those rates.

## 3. R2
- Pricing [docs], https://developers.cloudflare.com/r2/pricing/:

| Item | Price |
|---|---|
| Standard storage | $0.015/GB-month |
| Free storage | 10 GB-month |
| Class A operations | $4.50/M, first 1M/month free |
| Class B operations | $0.36/M, first 10M/month free |
| Infrequent Access storage | $0.01/GB-month |
| Egress | Free |

  - Infrequent Access operations cost $9.00/M (Class A) and $0.90/M (Class B).
  - Infrequent Access has a $0.01/GB retrieval fee and a 30-day minimum storage duration.

  - GET, HEAD, PUT and DELETE are supported.

  - `r2.dev` is rate-limited and meant for development only.
  - From a Worker, an R2 binding is also available; the Python Workers page lists R2 among supported bindings.

## 4. Cloudflare Containers (compute only)
- Pricing [docs], https://developers.cloudflare.com/containers/pricing/:
  - Workers Paid includes 25 GiB-hours of memory, 375 vCPU-minutes and 200 GB-hours of disk per month.
  - Overage is $0.0000025 per GiB-second of memory, $0.000020 per vCPU-second (active use only) and $0.00000007 per GB-second of disk.
  - Billing is per 10 ms of active running, and charges stop when the instance sleeps.
  - Egress is $0.025/GB in North America and Europe with 1 TB included.
  - Instance sizes run from lite (1/16 vCPU, 256 MiB, 2 GB disk) to standard-4 (4 vCPU, 12 GiB, 20 GB disk). I did not retrieve the intermediate sizes.
- Behaviour [docs]:
  - Cold starts are "often in the 1-3 second range".
  - `sleepAfter` defaults to 10 minutes.
  - Disk is ephemeral and resets on each start.

## 5. Workers Paid
- Pricing [docs], https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/platform/pricing/: $5/month per account. It includes:

  - 30M CPU-ms, then $0.02/M.

  - Hyperdrive queries: unlimited.

  - Volumes are about $0.15/GB-month and egress is $0.05/GB.

  - Hobby volumes are capped at 5 GB.

- App sleeping [docs], https://docs.railway.com/reference/app-sleeping:
  - A service sleeps after 5 minutes without outbound packets.
  - The first request after sleep can be slow or return a 502.
  - Persistent database connections or telemetry from the service block sleeping.

## 7. Monthly bill estimate (estimate, not a quote)

- Marginal bill: **$0**, with $5/month already sunk.
- If the API runs in a Container, assuming a 1 GiB, 4 GB-disk instance (my assumption; I did not retrieve that size's spec):
  - Memory is 20 h × 1 GiB = 20 GiB-h against 25 included.
  - Disk is 20 h × 4 GB = 80 GB-h against 200 included.
  - CPU is a few vCPU-minutes against 375 included.
  - Marginal cost is about $0.
  - For comparison, an always-on instance would cost about 2,628,000 GiB-s × $0.0000025 = $6.57 for memory, minus the 90,000 GiB-s included (about $0.23), plus about $0.74 for disk, so about $7.

- Postgres CPU, assuming 0.02 vCPU: 2,628,000 × 0.02 × $0.00000772 = $0.41.

- Bucket, 1 GB: $0.015.
- Usage is about $3.2, below the $5 credit.

content.text:
Moving the API, database and bucket is possible. The bucket move is a configuration change, the database move is a change of engine, and where the API code runs is a choice with three options. On cost, you'd save about $5/month (Railway's minimum fee); the Cloudflare side would be close to $0 extra because Workers Paid is already paid for the pipeline. Both figures are the researcher's estimates, not quotes.

**Current system:** it's drawn at http://localhost:5190. To ask for a change, put a sticky note on the shape (or draw an arrow from the note to it), then click "Send to Claude". I haven't drawn the Cloudflare version yet.

## What the API depends on today
These come from the code scout, with file references.
- **Runtime:** Python 3.12, FastAPI on uvicorn, deployed by Railway from `api/railway.toml`. Migrations run as a pre-deploy step (`alembic upgrade head`), and the app sleeps when idle.
- **Database:** Postgres through async SQLAlchemy and asyncpg, with 7 Alembic migrations. The schema already runs on SQLite in dev: 3 tables, JSON columns, no Postgres-only features. Concurrency control is a conditional `UPDATE … WHERE status = …` that checks the row count.
- **Storage:** an S3 bucket through boto3. Audio is one file per item and images are WebP. Clients get audio through a 307 redirect to a presigned URL; the API never streams the bytes.
- **Deferred work:**
  - The Firecrawl fetch and the extraction spawn run as a `BackgroundTasks` handler after the response, with no time limit.
  - Everything after that (extraction result, describing images, TTS, storing the audio) runs inside `GET /items/{id}` polls.
- **Modal:** called through the synchronous `modal` Python client, which uses gRPC. Audio comes back base64-encoded in the poll result.
- **Native dependencies:**
  - Pillow re-encodes images to WebP.
  - cairosvg needs the system cairo library. If it's missing, only SVG images are dropped.
- **Pipeline:** stores no recipes or articles. The API sends the current recipe with each job and keeps `recipe_versions` and `items` in its own Postgres.

## Where the API can run on Cloudflare
None of this was tried; it comes from Cloudflare's and Modal's documentation.

| | Python Workers | Containers | TypeScript Worker (rewrite) |
|---|---|---|---|
| FastAPI | Yes, through an ASGI adapter | Yes, unchanged | No, needs a JS framework |
| `modal` client | No: it needs grpcio, which Python Workers can't run | Yes | No |
| cairosvg | Not available | Yes | No |
| Pillow, httpx, SQLAlchemy | Available | Yes | npm equivalents needed |
| boto3, google-genai, firecrawl-py | Not bundled; whether they install is unverified | Yes | npm equivalents needed |
| Deferred work | `waitUntil` (30 s), Queues, Workflows | Runs in the process, as today | `waitUntil`, Queues, Workflows, DO alarms |
| D1 and R2 | Bindings | Not as bindings: D1's REST API, R2 over the S3 API, or a Worker in front as a proxy (unverified) | Bindings |
| Cold start | About 1 s (one third-party measurement) | Often 1–3 s; sleeps after 10 min idle by default | Milliseconds |

- **Python Workers status:** the two researchers disagree. One cites a GA announcement on 2026-09-21. The other read a docs page that still says beta behind the `python_workers` flag. They also mention Python 3.14 becoming the default from 2026-09-08. Neither checked whether 3.12 can still be pinned.
- **Modal without its Python client:** Modal has no public REST API for spawning a function and polling it. The documented pattern is to deploy your own web endpoints in the Modal app (`POST /submit`, `GET /result/{call_id}`), protected by proxy-auth tokens. That keeps the TTS on Modal but changes code in `tts/`.

## Data and files
- **The database has to change engine.** D1 is the only database Cloudflare hosts. Hyperdrive sits in front of an external Postgres and doesn't host one. So "the database on Cloudflare" means going from Postgres to SQLite.
  - D1 offers JSON functions, `meta.changes` for checking the conditional updates, and 30 days of point-in-time restore (Time Travel).
  - SQLAlchemy has a third-party D1 driver (`sqlalchemy-cloudflare-d1` 0.4.1, released 2026-10-02). Its own description says async is unavailable inside Workers, and the API uses async SQLAlchemy throughout.
  - Cloudflare documents `wrangler d1 migrations` with `.sql` files. Using Alembic against D1 is undocumented.
- **R2 should work with the existing storage code** given a new endpoint and credentials. R2 accepts boto3 with region `auto`, supports presigned GET URLs for up to 7 days (the API uses 1 hour), and charges no egress. Presigned URLs only work on the `*.r2.cloudflarestorage.com` host, not on a custom domain.

## Cost (the researcher's estimates)
Assumed workload: about 40 articles a month, about 1 GB of audio stored after 5 months, about 5,000 requests a month.

| | Monthly | Main cost |
|---|---|---|
| Railway (Hobby) | About $5, up to about $6–8 if Postgres uses more memory or the API doesn't sleep | The $5 minimum fee, then Postgres memory (always on) |
| Cloudflare | About $0 on top of the $5 Workers Paid plan | Everything fits in the included allowances |

A Container that sleeps fits inside the included hours. One that never sleeps would cost about $7 a month.

## Docs and invariants this changes
- **Invariant 5** (the Python API runs deferred work as `BackgroundTasks` and spawns Modal from the Python client) needs revisiting under any option except Containers.
- **Invariant 7** says Alembic owns the schema; that has to change unless Alembic works against D1.
- **Invariant 8** names Railway watch paths as what keeps the deployables independent.
- `deployment-and-ci.md` describes Railway's two dashboard-only settings and the DNS CNAME to Railway. `api/` would need a deploy job in CI like `pipeline/` has.
- No note records a hosting cost or the recipe-reconciliation reason for the move.

## Decisions this raises
1. Where does the API run: Python Workers, Containers, or a TypeScript rewrite?
2. If not Containers, does `tts/` gain HTTP endpoints for spawn and poll, or is there another way to reach Modal?
3. Is D1 (Postgres to SQLite) acceptable, or does "the database moves to Cloudflare" allow a Postgres behind Hyperdrive that lives somewhere else?
4. Do schema migrations stay on Alembic or move to `wrangler d1 migrations`?
5. What replaces `BackgroundTasks` for the Firecrawl-then-spawn step: `waitUntil` (30 s cap), a Queue, a Workflow, or the container process?
6. Do the existing Postgres rows and bucket files get copied over, or does the move start empty?
7. Is losing SVG images (cairosvg) acceptable under a Workers option?

The wiki has a `cloudflare` section (global and local) that I haven't read. I can check this direction against it if you want.

entries.name: Monitor
entries.description:
Start a background monitor that streams events from a long-running script. Each stdout line is an event — you keep working and notifications arrive in the chat. Events arrive on their own schedule and are not replies from the user, even if one lands while you're waiting for the user to answer a question.

Pick by how many notifications you need:
- **One** ("tell me when the server is ready / the build finishes") → use **Bash with `run_in_background`** and a command that exits when the condition is true, e.g. `until grep -q "Ready in" dev.log; do sleep 0.5; done`. You get a single completion notification when it exits.
- **One per occurrence, until the monitor expires (re-arm to continue)** ("tell me every time an ERROR line appears") → Monitor with an unbounded command (`tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, `while true`).
- **One per occurrence, until a known end** ("emit each CI step result, stop when the run completes") → Monitor with a command that emits lines and then exits.

Your script's stdout is the event stream. Each line becomes a notification. Exit ends the watch.

  # Each matching log line is an event
  tail -f /var/log/app.log | grep --line-buffered "ERROR"

  # Each file change is an event
  inotifywait -m --format '%e %f' /watched/dir

  # Poll GitHub for new PR comments and emit one line per new comment
  last=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
  while true; do
    now=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
    gh api "repos/owner/repo/issues/123/comments?since=$last" --jq '.[] | "\(.user.login): \(.body)"'
    last=$now; sleep 30
  done

  # Node script that emits events as they arrive (e.g. WebSocket listener)
  node watch-for-events.js

  # Per-occurrence with a natural end: emit each CI check as it lands, exit when the run completes
  prev=""
  while true; do
    s=$(gh pr checks 123 --json name,bucket)
    cur=$(jq -r '.[] | select(.bucket!="pending") | "\(.name): \(.bucket)"' <<<"$s" | sort)
    comm -13 <(echo "$prev") <(echo "$cur")
    prev=$cur
    jq -e 'all(.bucket!="pending")' <<<"$s" >/dev/null && break
    sleep 30
  done

**Don't use an unbounded command for a single notification.** `tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, and `while true` never exit on their own, so the monitor stays armed until timeout even after the event has fired. For "tell me when X is ready," use Bash `run_in_background` with an `until` loop instead (one notification, ends in seconds). Note that `tail -f log | grep -m 1 ...` does *not* fix this: if the log goes quiet after the match, `tail` never receives SIGPIPE and the pipeline hangs anyway.

**Script quality:**
- Every pipe stage must flush per line or matches sit in its buffer unseen: `grep` needs `--line-buffered`, `awk` needs `fflush()`. `head` cannot flush at all — `| head -N` delivers nothing until N matches accumulate, then ends the stream.
- In poll loops, handle transient failures (`curl ... || true`) — one failed request shouldn't kill the monitor.
- Poll intervals: 30s+ for remote APIs (rate limits), 0.5-1s for local checks.
- Write a specific `description` — it appears in every notification ("errors in deploy.log" not "watching logs").
- Only stdout is the event stream. Stderr goes to the output file (readable via Read) but does not trigger notifications — for a command you run directly (e.g. `python train.py 2>&1 | grep --line-buffered ...`), merge stderr with `2>&1` so its failures reach your filter. (No effect on `tail -f` of an existing log — that file only contains what its writer redirected.)

**Coverage — silence is not success.** When watching a job or process for an outcome, your filter must match every terminal state, not just the happy path. A monitor that greps only for the success marker stays silent through a crashloop, a hung process, or an unexpected exit — and silence looks identical to "still running." Before arming, ask: *if this process crashed right now, would my filter emit anything?* If not, widen it.

  # Wrong — silent on crash, hang, or any non-success exit
  tail -f run.log | grep --line-buffered "elapsed_steps="

  # Right — one alternation covering progress + the failure signatures you'd act on
  tail -f run.log | grep -E --line-buffered "elapsed_steps=|Traceback|Error|FAILED|assert|Killed|OOM"

For poll loops checking job state, emit on every terminal status (`succeeded|failed|cancelled|timeout`), not just success. If you cannot confidently enumerate the failure signatures, broaden the grep alternation rather than narrow it — some extra noise is better than missing a crashloop.

**Output volume**: Every stdout line is a conversation message, so the filter should be selective — but selective means "the lines you'd act on," not "only good news." Never pipe raw logs; filter to exactly the success and failure signals you care about. Monitors that produce too many events are automatically stopped; restart with a tighter filter if this happens.

Stdout lines within 200ms are batched into a single notification, so multiline output from a single event groups naturally.

The script runs in the same shell environment as Bash. Exit ends the watch (exit code is reported). Every monitor expires after `timeout_ms` (default 5 minutes, at most 30 minutes): it is killed and you get one notice with the event count. Re-arm it if you still need the watch; for a long watch (PR monitoring, log tails) set `timeout_ms` to the maximum and re-arm on each expiry, and widen the filter if an expiry with no events was unexpected. Use TaskStop to cancel early.
**ws source** — open a WebSocket and stream each incoming text frame as an event. No shell, no polling: the server pushes, you get notified.

  Monitor({
    ws: {url: 'wss://events.example.com/stream', protocols: ['v1']},
    description: 'deploy events',
  })

Each text frame becomes one notification (multiline frames stay as one event). Binary frames are reported as `[binary frame, N bytes]` rather than passed through. Socket close ends the watch with the close code surfaced; errors are surfaced before close. Same rate limiting as bash — a firehose will be suppressed and eventually stopped, so subscribe to a filtered feed where one exists.

Prefer this over `command: 'websocat wss://…'` — it avoids the extra process and line-buffering pitfalls. Use bash when you need to transform or filter frames with shell tools before they become events.

description.description: Short human-readable description of what you are monitoring (shown in notifications).

timeout_ms.description: Kill the monitor after this deadline. Default 300000ms. Deadlines above 1800000ms are capped to 1800000ms. You are notified at expiry and can re-arm.

command.description: Shell command or script. Each stdout line is an event; exit ends the watch.

ws.description: WebSocket to open. Each text frame is an event; binary frames are reported as a placeholder line. Socket close ends the watch. Cannot be combined with command.

**Canvas notes:** a watch was running and it logged both of your "Send to Claude" clicks. It didn't wake me, though, because it ran as a plain background command that only notifies when it exits. It now runs as a monitor, so each click reaches me as it happens. I applied both notes: the stores are now labeled **Railway Postgres** and **Railway bucket (S3-compatible)**, and I deleted the notes.

**2. Why `tts/` would need new endpoints.** The API reaches Modal through the `modal` Python package, and that package talks to Modal over gRPC. A Python Worker can't install gRPC, and a TypeScript Worker has no Modal client at all, so from either one the only way to reach Modal is a plain HTTP request. Modal doesn't offer a ready-made HTTP API for "start this function" and "check this call by id". The documented approach is to add two small web endpoints to the Modal app yourself:
- one that starts synthesis and returns the call id
- one that returns the result for a call id, or "still running"

The GPU function itself stays as it is. With Containers none of this is needed, because the container can run the `modal` package unchanged.

**5. Cloudflare services for the Firecrawl-then-spawn step.** These come from the earlier research; nothing was tried:
- **Queues:** the API sends a message and a consumer Worker does the work. Each consumer run gets up to 15 minutes, and failed messages are retried.
- **Workflows:** a durable job made of steps, with retries per step. The pipeline already uses one for extraction.
- **Durable Object alarms:** an object schedules itself to wake up and do the work later.
- **`waitUntil`:** the work continues after the response, but only for 30 seconds.

The first three move the work out of the API's request. So `queued_at` and the retry route would no longer exist to recover work that died with the container (invariant 5 today).

**4. Migrations:** a researcher is looking up the new Cloudflare CLI: what it is, how it compares with wrangler for D1 migrations, deploys and CI, and whether Alembic can drive D1 at all. Neither earlier researcher found documentation of Alembic working against D1, and the only SQLAlchemy D1 driver says async isn't available inside Workers.

**1. Testing all three runtimes:** building and running throwaway code against Cloudflare is a spike, which is `mahou:spike`'s job, not this exploration's. I can open it when you're ready. Before that, the order of the parts needs settling. These are the parts the research left unverified:
- runs FastAPI
- converts SVG and re-encodes WebP (cairosvg and Pillow)
- reads and writes D1 (and Alembic, for the Python options)
- writes to R2 and returns a presigned URL
- spawns and polls Modal
- runs the deferred step
- cold start

Decisions:
1. `api/` moves to Cloudflare.
2. The database moves to Cloudflare.
3. The file bucket moves to Cloudflare.
4. Railway stops being used for nagara.
5. `tts/` stays on Modal.
6. The database switches from Postgres to SQLite (D1).
7. The move starts empty: no rows or files are copied from Railway.
8. SVG images must keep working.
9. The runtime is chosen by trying all three (Python Workers, Containers, a TypeScript Worker) against Cloudflare, one part at a time, with subagents.
10. Migrations stay on Alembic if the API stays in Python; otherwise open, with the new Cloudflare CLI to be evaluated.

Questions for you:
- Which of those parts go into the spike, and in what order?
- For the deferred step, which of Queues, Workflows, Durable Object alarms or `waitUntil` should the spike try?

{"pane_id":"w3W:pB","label":"research: new cloudflare cli","agent":"research-new-cloudflare-cli","status":"done","message":"## 1. `cf` (the new Cloudflare CLI)

URL: https://github.com/cloudflare/cf · announcement https://blog.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-cf-cli-launch/ (fetched through the mirror at noise.getoto.net)

- **Identity**
  - The npm package is `cf` (binaries `cf` and `cloudflare`). The latest is `1.0.0-beta.12`, published 2026-10-02 (registry.npmjs.org, verified). Licence is MIT OR Apache-2.0.
  - Open beta announced 2026-09-28 (announcement mirror; the blog itself did not load for me). The package README links a second post, `blog.cloudflare.com/cf-cli-local-explorer/`, which describes a "technical preview" via `npx cf`. The two posts disagree on the label.
  - It is actively maintained: 12 betas in about a week, and the repository was pushed to on 2026-10-04 (GitHub API).
- **C1 (status, relation to wrangler)**
  - Open beta. Cloudflare describes it as the successor and eventual replacement for wrangler (announcement; documentation-level).
  - When the beta ends, Cloudflare ships a final wrangler major that points users to `cf`, then gives 18 months of maintenance (announcement).
  - `cf migrate` converts a wrangler project (trial: `--dry-run`, `--bundler vite|wrangler`).
  - Its API surface is generated from the OpenAPI schema, about 3,000 operations against wrangler's roughly 280 (announcement).
- **C2 (D1 migrations)**
  - Trial: `cf d1 migrations` exists, described as "Create, list, and apply D1 database migrations".
  - The README says `--local` supports "D1 raw plus D1 migration list/apply". I could not read the flags of the subcommands, because `-h` on them printed the root help.
  - Not verified: file format, tracking table, rollback, and whether `create` works locally.
  - `cf d1 time-travel` exists (trial).
- **C3 (deploy, bindings)**
  - Trial: `cf deploy` has `--prebuilt`, `--tag`, `--message`, `--secrets-file`, `--dry-run`, `--dispatch-namespace` and `--containers-rollout immediate|gradual|none`. `cf containers` and `cf workers versions create` also exist.
  - Config moves to a typed `cloudflare.config.ts`, with a `bindings` helper that lists D1, R2, KV, Queues, Vectorize, AI and worker-to-worker bindings (announcement). Workflows bindings in the config are not confirmed.
  - The default build tool is Vite. The announcement says `cf` "will continue to delegate builds to Wrangler" for projects that need it, with Python Workers named as an example. It documents no Python Worker flow.
  - The `cf init` template is a TypeScript Worker (README).

content.text:
The research contradicts part of decision 10: staying in Python doesn't by itself keep Alembic working. The only SQLAlchemy driver for D1 has no Alembic support and no transactions. Alembic's offline mode (`alembic upgrade --sql`) could write migrations as SQL files for D1's own migration commands, but no one has tried that yet.

**Alembic against D1**
- `sqlalchemy-cloudflare-d1` 0.4.1 was published 2026-10-02; 0.4.0 came out on 2026-09-19. The project has 24 stars. The researcher inspected the 0.4.1 package and found no Alembic code in it.
- Its README says every statement commits on its own, and its `commit` and `rollback` do nothing. A migration that fails halfway would leave the schema half-applied.
- No other package connects Alembic to D1. A separate `sqlalchemy-d1` project pins SQLAlchemy below 2.0, and the API uses SQLAlchemy 2.

**The new CLI, `cf`**
- It's an open beta, announced 2026-09-28; the latest release is `1.0.0-beta.12` from 2026-10-02. A second Cloudflare post calls it a "technical preview".
- Cloudflare presents it as the eventual replacement for wrangler. When the beta ends, wrangler gets a final major release and 18 more months of maintenance.
- `cf migrate` converts a wrangler project. The configuration becomes a typed `cloudflare.config.ts`.
- It has a `cf d1 migrations` command, but the researcher couldn't read its flags or file format.
- For Python Workers, `cf` hands the build to wrangler. It documents no Python flow of its own, and its project template is a TypeScript Worker.
- It runs locally against Miniflare (D1, R2, KV). It has no official GitHub Action yet. It authenticates with `CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN`, as wrangler does.

**wrangler**
- It's GA. The latest is 4.147.0; the pipeline pins 4.135.0.
- D1 migrations are hand-written `.sql` files tracked in a `d1_migrations` table, applied with `--local` or `--remote`. A failed migration is rolled back on its own, but there is no command to undo an applied migration; restoring with Time Travel is the only way back.
- Python Workers deploy through `pywrangler`. Its GitHub Action is `wrangler-action` v4.1.3.

The settled decisions are unchanged.

Questions this raises:
- For the Python options, should the spike try Alembic writing SQL files for D1's migration commands, or should migrations move to hand-written SQL?
- Should the spike deploy with `cf` (beta, hands Python builds to wrangler) or with wrangler?

The two questions about the spike from my last message, which parts and which deferred-work service, are still open.

Decisions: 1. `api/` moves to Cloudflare. 2. The database moves to Cloudflare. 3. The file bucket moves to Cloudflare. 4. Railway stops being used for nagara. 5. `tts/` stays on Modal. 6. The database switches from Postgres to SQLite (D1). 7. The move starts empty: no rows or files are copied from Railway. 8. SVG images must keep working. 9. The runtime is chosen by trying all three (Python Workers, Containers, a TypeScript Worker) against Cloudflare, one part at a time, with subagents. 10. The spike tries both migration approaches on the Python options: Alembic writing SQL files for D1's migration commands, and hand-written SQL migrations. 11. The spike deploys with wrangler, not `cf`. 12. The spike tests every part on every runtime: FastAPI or its replacement, SVG and WebP, D1, R2 with a presigned URL, Modal, the deferred step, and cold start. ## The three runtimes Everything below comes from documentation; nothing has been run yet. | | Pros | Cons | |---|---|---| | **Python Workers** | • The FastAPI code stays (ASGI adapter)
• D1, R2, Workflows, Queues and service bindings are native
• Scales to zero; no container to keep warm
• Pillow and SQLAlchemy are in Pyodide | • No cairosvg: SVG needs another route, and SVG is a hard requirement now
• No `modal` client: `tts/` gains the two HTTP endpoints
• boto3, google-genai, firecrawl-py and markdown-it-py aren't bundled; whether they install is unverified
• The D1 driver has no async inside Workers, and the API is async throughout
• Each isolate gets 128 MB of memory, including image re-encoding
• Status is either just GA (2026-09-21) or still beta; the sources disagree
• Python 3.14 is the default; pinning 3.12 is unverified | | **Containers** | • The app runs unchanged: cairosvg, Pillow, the `modal` client, boto3, `BackgroundTasks`
• Cold start is 1–3 s and the container sleeps after 10 min idle, close to Railway's behavior
• The included hours cover this workload | • D1 isn't reachable as a binding: it's the REST API, or a Worker in front acting as a proxy (unverified)
• Every container sits behind a Durable Object and a Worker, two extra layers
• Using Workflows or Queues for deferred work also means calling them through that Worker
• Disk is wiped on sleep (the API keeps nothing local in production, so this is a fact rather than a problem) | | **TypeScript Worker** | • Same runtime and language as `pipeline/`: shared tooling, native bindings, millisecond cold starts
• Workflows, Queues and Durable Object alarms are all native
• The extraction call becomes a service binding instead of Cloudflare Access over the public internet | • A full rewrite of `api/`
• SVG and WebP need npm or WASM equivalents (not researched)
• No Modal client: `tts/` gains the two HTTP endpoints
• Gemini, Firecrawl and S3 presigning need JS libraries (not researched)
• Migrations become hand-written SQL; Alembic leaves with Python | ## The deferred-work services These come from the earlier research; Workflows' own limits haven't been looked up yet. | | Pros | Cons | |---|---|---| | **`waitUntil`** | • Simplest: the request handler keeps going after the response | • Capped at 30 s, and the Firecrawl step has no upper bound
• Work that dies still needs `queued_at` and the retry route to recover | | **Queues** | • Retried messages; each consumer run gets up to 15 min
• Fits "do this one step later" | • One message is one unit of work: a multi-step flow chains messages, or tracks its own state | | **Workflows** | • Durable steps with a retry per step; a crash resumes from the last finished step
• The pipeline already uses one, so the team knows it | • Python access to Workflows is reported but unverified
• Limits on step count, step output size and sleep aren't researched; audio comes back from Modal base64-encoded in one poll, so the output size limit matters | | **Durable Object alarms** | • One object per item could hold that item's state and wake itself to poll | • You write the retries and the scheduling yourself
• From a Container it goes through the Worker in front | ## One Workflow for the whole item It could be done: fetch, extract, describe, TTS, then store, as steps of one durable run instead of the API advancing the item on each `GET /items/{id}`. What that would change: - **Status updates:** the item's state would be written to D1 by the Workflow, and polling would become a read. - **Invariant 5:** "no worker, deferred work dies with the container" stops being true; Workflows' durable retries replace `queued_at` and the retry route. - **Where the Workflow lives:** the extraction Workflow is in `pipeline/`, so one Workflow spanning both `api/` and `pipeline/` sits across two deployables. Today's invariant 8 keeps those shipping independently. The other option is a Workflow in the API that calls the extraction Workflow as one step. - **Per-domain queue:** `DomainQueue` puts jobs for the same domain in a line ahead of extraction. A merged Workflow would have to wait on it, or the queue would move. - **Modal:** a Workflow step would sleep and poll Modal, so either the `modal` client or the HTTP endpoints would have to be reachable from where that step runs. Questions this raises: - Does the item Workflow live in `api/`, in `pipeline/`, or does the split between the two change? - Should I research Workflows' limits (step output size, step count, sleep, calling from Python) before the spike?

I've drawn the four options at http://localhost:5190 (the current system is saved in its own file). Each one combines a runtime with a way to run the deferred work. A watch is running, so a "Send to Claude" click reaches me as it happens.

- **A. Python Worker + Workflows**
- **B. Python Worker + Queues**
- **C. Container + Workflows**
- **D. Container + Queues**

**Moving the item Workflow into `pipeline/` partly conflicts with dropping the TypeScript Worker.** `pipeline/` is TypeScript, so a Workflow there runs describing, image processing (SVG and WebP) and the TTS call in TypeScript. The other way is for each of those steps to call back into the Python API. The canvas notes this in A and C.

**This also affects the TTS call in A and C.** A step inside the Workflow can't use the `modal` Python client, so in C `tts/` still needs the two HTTP endpoints even though the API runs in a container. D is the only option where Modal is still called exactly as it is today.

Decisions:
1. `api/` moves to Cloudflare.
2. The database moves to Cloudflare.
3. The file bucket moves to Cloudflare.
4. Railway stops being used for nagara.
5. `tts/` stays on Modal.
6. The database switches from Postgres to SQLite (D1).
7. The move starts empty: no rows or files are copied from Railway.
8. SVG images must keep working.
9. The runtime is chosen by trying Python Workers and Containers against Cloudflare, one part at a time, with subagents. The TypeScript Worker is dropped.
10. The spike tries both migration approaches on the Python options: Alembic writing SQL files for D1's migration commands, and hand-written SQL migrations.
11. The spike deploys with wrangler, not `cf`.
12. The spike tests every part on both runtimes: FastAPI, SVG and WebP, D1, R2 with a presigned URL, Modal, the deferred step, and cold start.
13. For the deferred work, the spike tries Queues and Workflows.
14. If Workflows is used, the item Workflow lives in `pipeline/`.
15. The spike finds Workflows' limits (step output size, step count, sleep, calling from Python) itself, rather than through separate research first.

Questions for you:
- In the Workflow options, do describing, image processing and the TTS call get written in TypeScript inside `pipeline/`, or does each step call back into the Python API?
- In the Queue options, does the consumer stay in the API (the Python Worker in B, the front Worker passing work to the container in D), or move to `pipeline/` as well?

content.text:
I made all three changes on http://localhost:5190, and deleted your sticky note.

- **Today's system:** copied onto the top of this canvas, so you can see it and the four options at once.
- **Item Workflow, step by step:** drawn at the bottom. It applies to options A and C:
  1. fetch the page with Firecrawl
  2. wait for the domain's lease (DomainQueue)
  3. run the recipe, with the Flue agents writing or revising it; a new recipe version goes to D1
  4. images: fetch them, convert SVG to PNG, re-encode as WebP, store in R2
  5. describe the images with Gemini
  6. start the TTS on Modal
  7. sleep and check the TTS until it finishes
  8. store the audio in R2, then write the units, timing, cost and `ready` to D1

  Each step writes the item's status to D1, so `GET /items/{id}` only reads it.
- **Separate consumers in the queue options:**
  - In **B**, the API Worker only sends steps to the queue. A separate Python Worker reads them and calls Firecrawl, Gemini, the image hosts, extraction, Modal, R2 and D1.
  - In **D**, the API container only sends steps to the queue. A separate container behind its own front Worker reads them, with the `modal` client, cairosvg and Pillow.

The step order in the Workflow is my reading of today's code, rearranged into one sequence. Two placements are mine: image processing as its own step after extraction, and the recipe-version write at step 3. The code does both inside the extraction result step.

1. `api/` moves to Cloudflare.
2. The database moves to Cloudflare.
3. The file bucket moves to Cloudflare.
4. Railway stops being used for nagara.
5. `tts/` stays on Modal.
6. The database switches from Postgres to SQLite (D1).
7. The move starts empty: no rows or files are copied from Railway.
8. SVG images must keep working.
9. The runtime is chosen by trying Python Workers and Containers against Cloudflare, one part at a time, with subagents. The TypeScript Worker is dropped.
10. The spike tries both migration approaches on the Python options: Alembic writing SQL files for D1's migration commands, and hand-written SQL migrations.
11. The spike deploys with wrangler, not `cf`.
12. The spike tests every part on both runtimes: FastAPI, SVG and WebP, D1, R2 with a presigned URL, Modal, the deferred step, and cold start.
13. For the deferred work, the spike tries Queues and Workflows.
14. If Workflows is used, the item Workflow lives in `pipeline/`.
15. The spike finds Workflows' limits (step output size, step count, sleep, calling from Python) itself, rather than through separate research first.
16. In the Queue options, the consumer is a separate Worker (B) or a separate container (D), not the API.

Still open:
- In the Workflow options, do describing, image processing and the TTS call get written in TypeScript inside `pipeline/`, or does each step call back into the Python API?
- Do the queue consumers in B and D live in `api/`, in `pipeline/`, or in a deployable of their own?

I applied three of your four notes on the canvas:
- **Spacing:** option C's full diagram now has room below its title.
- **External services:** Firecrawl, the image hosts, Gemini and Modal are clouds in every drawing, not only option C.
- **Client:** it's an ellipse everywhere, so squares are only our own modules.

**The note beside option C's full diagram is gone.** It was the one saying every step writes status to D1 and image processing runs in the Workflow. I didn't delete it on purpose, and I can't tell whether you removed it or my cleanup of the sticky notes did. I can put it back.

**Your other note asked whether the API could become TypeScript too, since it's thin. Yes: if the Workflow does all the item work, almost nothing is left that needs Python.** Under option C with the full Workflow, the API keeps five jobs:
- checking `X-API-Key`
- `POST /items`: insert a row in D1 and start the Workflow
- `GET /items/{id}`: read the row from D1
- the audio and image routes: redirect to a presigned R2 URL
- `POST /items/{id}/retry`

Everything that tied the API to Python moves into the Workflow under that option: the `modal` client, cairosvg and Pillow, `firecrawl-py` and `google-genai`. What a TypeScript API Worker would change:
- It reaches D1 and the Workflow directly through bindings, with no front Worker, Durable Object or container in between.
- It runs in the same language and tooling as `pipeline/`.
- Two things are unresearched: presigning R2 URLs from TypeScript, and whether an R2 binding can presign at all.

Two settled decisions conflict with this:
- **Decision 9 dropped the TypeScript Worker.** A TypeScript API would reopen it.
- **Decision 10 assumes the API stays in Python.** A TypeScript API ends Alembic, so migrations would be hand-written SQL for wrangler.

**"Thin" also depends on a question that's still open.** The API is only this thin if describing and the TTS call also run in the Workflow; if they call back into the Python API, that work stays in the API.

The settled set hasn't changed.

Questions this raises:
- Is the TypeScript API a fifth option to draw and spike next to A–D, or does it replace C?
- Do describing and the TTS call run in the Workflow, in TypeScript?

## 1. TypeScript/JavaScript Workflows
https://developers.cloudflare.com/workflows/build/workers-api/

- **W1:**
  - The Workflow class is authored by extending `WorkflowEntrypoint` and implementing `run(event, step)`. [docs]
  - It is the reference implementation: `step.do` (retries and rollback config), `step.sleep`, `step.sleepUntil` and `step.waitForEvent` (default timeout 24h, resumed by `instance.sendEvent()`). [docs]
  - Status: public beta from 2024-10-23, GA from 2025-04-07. [docs, changelog]
  - A Workflow can also be declared in `exports` with `type: "workflow"` and called through `ctx.exports.<Name>`. [docs]
- **W2:**
  - A cross-script Workflow binding uses the `script_name` field, so a Worker in another script can bind to this Workflow. [docs]
  - Service bindings are asynchronous and must be awaited. [docs] The service bindings page does not say which Worker languages can sit on either side.
  - No page says whether a binding from a non-JS Worker to a JS Workflow is supported or unsupported.

## 2. Python Workflows (Python Workers)
https://developers.cloudflare.com/workflows/python/

- **W1:**
  - The Workflow class can be authored in Python by exporting a `WorkflowEntrypoint` (`from workers import WorkflowEntrypoint`) with `async def run(self, event, step)`. [docs, last updated 2026-09-17]
  - Steps are declared as `@step.do('name', config={...})`, with `concurrent` and `depends=[...]` options. Implicit dependency resolution by parameter name is preferred for new Workflows. `step.sleep`, `step.sleep_until` and `step.wait_for_event` (24h default timeout) exist. [docs, python-workers-api page]
  - Status: "Python Workflows is now in open beta" on 2025-08-22. [docs, changelog] No later GA entry appears in the changelog I fetched. The Python SDK pages state no status.
- **W2:**
  - A Python Worker creates instances with `await self.env.MY_WORKFLOW.create()`, "like you would on a JavaScript worker". `env` is a JsProxy of the JS object. [docs]
  - The docs state no restriction on Python/JS interop. They also state no explicit support for a Python Worker binding to a JS Workflow, or the reverse.

## 3. Other languages
- **Rust via workers-rs**
  - **W1:** No. `WorkflowEntrypoint` is not supported in workers-rs. The "Workflows support" issue #663 has been open since 2024-10-25. [source] PR #918 "feat: add Workflows support" (opened 2026-01-28) is open and unmerged, last updated 2026-09-18. [source] The latest workers-rs release is v0.8.7, published 2026-09-25. [source] The Rust docs page I grepped lists no Workflow binding type. [docs]
  - **W2:** A Rust Worker can be called by a Workflow step through a service binding (the generic mechanism). I did not find this documented for Rust specifically.
- **WASM-compiled code**
  - The Workflows docs list no WASM-authored Workflow. I found no page that says either way. A TypeScript Workflow could call a WASM module in-process from a step. I did not verify this.
- **Container called from a step**
  - **W1:** Not applicable. A container does not author the Workflow class.
  - **W2:**
    - Containers are reached through a Durable Object binding: `getContainer(env.X, id)`, or `ctx.container` inside a `DurableObject`. [docs]
    - The Workflows docs I fetched do not mention Containers or call one from a step. The Containers docs I fetched did not state GA or beta status, or which Worker languages can invoke them. A step can call the Durable Object binding like any other binding, but that is an inference, not a documented claim.

## W3: Limits (apply to all Workflows, language-independent) [docs, limits page, last updated 2026-09-21]

| Limit | Free | Paid |
|---|---|---|
| Non-stream step result | 1 MiB | 1 MiB |
| Steps per instance | 1,024 | 10,000 default, configurable up to 25,000 |
| Max sleep | 365 days | 365 days |
| CPU time per step | 10 ms | 30 s default, configurable up to 5 min |
| Wall time per step | unlimited | unlimited |
| Retention of completed instance state | 3 days | 30 days |
| State size per instance | 100 MB | 1 GB |
| Concurrent instances | 100 | 50,000 (waiting instances don't count) |
| Subrequests per request | 50 | 10,000 default, up to 10 million |

- Event payload is limited to 1 MiB.
- Paid plans can create 300 instances per second per account, and have a 2,000,000 queued-instance cap.
- `step.sleep` does not count toward the step limit. [docs]
- JS steps can return a `ReadableStream<Uint8Array>` for large binary output (changelog 2026-03-26). That output is excluded from the 1 MiB limit, which applies to "non-stream" results. [docs]
- The limits page does not distinguish JS from Python. Whether the Python SDK supports stream returns is unverified.

## Cross-cutting
- Every Workflow runs on Workers. The class is authored in JS/TS or Python only; Rust is not supported.
- A step is ordinary Worker code. Anything it can reach through bindings (service bindings, Durable Object bindings, R2, D1, `fetch` to Modal) is available regardless of the language on the other side.

## Not verified
- Whether Python Workflows is still beta as of 2026-10-04. No GA entry was found, and the SDK pages state no status.
- Whether a Workflow binding crosses languages (Python Worker to JS Workflow, or the reverse) in practice. No trial was run.
- Whether Python steps support stream returns or the paid CPU-limit settings.
- The GA/beta status of Containers, and whether the Workflows docs mention calling them from a step.
- Whether workers-rs PR #918 will merge. Its status is only what is stated above.
- Whether Python Workers (not Workflows) carry a beta label. The grep of that page returned no matches for "beta".","ask":false}

content.text:
Workflows can be written in TypeScript/JavaScript or Python. Rust, WebAssembly and containers can't define a Workflow, but a step can call out to code in any language. None of this was tried; it comes from Cloudflare's docs and GitHub.

**By language**
- **TypeScript/JavaScript:** GA since 2025-04-07, with the full step API (`step.do`, `step.sleep`, `step.waitForEvent`). The pipeline already uses it.
- **Python:** open beta since 2025-08-22, and the researcher found no later GA entry.
  - It has the same step API, written with Python decorators (`@step.do`, `step.sleep`, `step.wait_for_event`).
  - It runs on Python Workers (Pyodide), with that package list: Pillow is there, while cairosvg and the `modal` client aren't.
- **Rust:** not supported. The workers-rs issue asking for Workflows has been open since 2024-10-25, and the pull request adding it hasn't been merged.
- **WebAssembly:** the docs don't mention it either way.

**Mixing languages**
- A step is ordinary Worker code. It can call anything it has a binding for: another Worker in another language, a Container through its Durable Object, R2, D1, or a plain HTTP request to Modal.
- A Workflow can be started from a Worker in a different script.
- Whether that works across languages (a Python Worker starting a TypeScript Workflow, or the reverse) isn't documented either way.
- A step calling a Container isn't described in the docs either. It should work through the Durable Object binding, but that's my inference.

**Limits that apply to option C**

| | Paid plan |
|---|---|
| Value a step returns | 1 MiB, but a JS step can return a stream instead, which doesn't count toward that limit |
| Steps per instance | 10,000 by default, up to 25,000 |
| CPU time per step | 30 s by default, up to 5 min |
| Wall time per step | Unlimited |
| Longest sleep | 365 days; sleeps don't count as steps |
| How long finished instances are kept | 30 days |

**Two of these limits matter for option C's steps:**
- **Audio:** Modal returns the audio base64-encoded in the poll result, and a few MB of audio is over 1 MiB. The poll step would have to write it to R2 itself, or return it as a stream.
- **Image processing:** the 30 s CPU default limits how long one step can spend converting and re-encoding images.

The settled set is unchanged.

Questions this raises:
- Is the item Workflow written in TypeScript, like the rest of `pipeline/`, or in Python?
- Image processing runs in the Workflow (decision 17). Does that mean in-process in a step, or a step that calls the API container to do it with cairosvg and Pillow?

I redrew option C as its own drawing, **Chosen: TypeScript API + item Workflow**, to the right of the earlier full C. It has no fallback image container. The API is a TypeScript Worker in `api/` that reaches D1 through a binding and starts the item Workflow in `pipeline/` through a Workflow binding. I left out the dashed `api/` box around it because it rendered clipped; the label says `api/` instead.

Decisions:
1. `api/` moves to Cloudflare.
2. The database moves to Cloudflare.
3. The file bucket moves to Cloudflare.
4. Railway stops being used for nagara.
5. `tts/` stays on Modal.
6. The database switches from Postgres to SQLite (D1).
7. The move starts empty: no rows or files are copied from Railway.
8. SVG images must keep working.
9. The spike deploys with wrangler, not `cf`.
10. The item Workflow lives in `pipeline/`.
11. The spike finds Workflows' limits (step output size, step count, sleep) itself, rather than through separate research first.
12. Image processing (SVG to PNG, WebP) is a step of the item Workflow. The spike checks whether it can run in TypeScript inside a Worker. If it can't, it runs in a container of its own, separate from the API.
13. The design to pursue is the **Chosen: TypeScript API + item Workflow** drawing. The spike covers only its unknowns.
14. Everything nagara runs on Cloudflare is TypeScript: the API, the item Workflow and the pipeline. `tts/` stays in Python on Modal.
15. Schema migrations are hand-written SQL files applied with wrangler.
16. The Workflow reaches Modal over HTTP, so `tts/` gains two web endpoints, one to start synthesis and one to fetch the result.
17. The API stays a separate deployable in `api/`, outside `pipeline/`.
18. The modules inside `pipeline/` may be reorganized to keep each part separate.

## Unknowns in the chosen design
1. **Image processing in a TypeScript Worker.** Can WebAssembly libraries turn SVG into PNG and re-encode to WebP inside a Worker? The limits that apply are 128 MB of memory per isolate, 30 s of CPU per step by default (5 min at most), and the bundle size cap. If not, the fallback container from decision 12 is used.
2. **Modal over HTTP.** This needs two web endpoints in `tts/` and a way to protect them. Audio comes back base64-encoded and is larger than the 1 MiB a step can return. So either the polling step writes it to R2 itself, or it returns it as a stream.
3. **Shape of the item Workflow.** This covers how the sleep-and-poll loop counts against the step limit, and the retry settings for each step. It also covers how step 2 waits for the domain's lease: DomainQueue was built to start one extraction Workflow per job, not to hold the lease for a step inside another Workflow.
4. **Starting a Workflow from another deployable.** The API Worker starts the item Workflow in `pipeline/` through a Workflow binding that names the other script. This has to work in production, in local development, and whichever of the two deploys first.
5. **One D1 database written by two Workers.** It's bound in both `api/` and `pipeline/`. Open points are the conditional updates (`meta.changes`), which deployable owns the hand-written migrations, and how they're applied in CI.
6. **Presigned R2 URLs from TypeScript.** It's unknown which library signs them, and whether an `<audio>` element plays the URL after the API's 307 redirect.
7. **Gemini and Firecrawl from a Worker.** Their JavaScript SDKs, or plain requests, have to run inside Workers.
8. **Local development and tests.** Both Workers would run locally with D1 and R2 simulated, with the binding between them working. The current test suite replays HTTP calls through vcrpy; a TypeScript suite would need a replacement.

Rewriting the spoken-form logic and the item contract in TypeScript isn't on this list. That's porting work, not an unknown. The invariants it has to keep (1–3, on how units and timing line up) carry over unchanged.

## How the spike would run
- **Coordinator:** one Opus subagent in its own herdr tab. It hands each unknown to a child subagent, runs the independent ones in parallel, collects the results, and writes one report into the change's scratch folder.
- **Children:** one per unknown, each with its own throwaway worktree and branch, deploying to Cloudflare under spike-only names. Each reports whether its unknown works, what it measured, and what failed.
- **Order:** unknowns 1, 2, 6 and 7 don't depend on anything and can run in parallel. 3, 4 and 5 build on each other. 8 comes last, once the pieces exist.
- **Throwaway:** spike code never merges. What it settles goes back to you as findings.

Running this is `mahou:spike`'s job, not this exploration's. I can open it once the plan is settled.

Questions for the plan:
- Are all eight unknowns in, or do some wait?
- Does the spike deploy to the real Cloudflare account under spike names and a separate Modal app (for example `nagara-tts-spike`), and who removes those resources afterwards, the coordinator or you?
- Does the spike use the real Gemini and Firecrawl keys, or record and replay responses?
- In decision 18, does "keep each part separate" mean the extraction steps and the item Workflow get separate modules inside `pipeline/`, or something else?

content.text:
I've sent a scout to find out how `pipeline/` and `api/` are tested today, including the cassettes, so I can answer your testing question from the code.

The local wiki also has a `testing` entry on how the test suites replay the services behind HTTP boundaries. I can read it if you want.

Decisions:
1. `api/` moves to Cloudflare.
2. The database moves to Cloudflare.
3. The file bucket moves to Cloudflare.
4. Railway stops being used for nagara.
5. `tts/` stays on Modal.
6. The database switches from Postgres to SQLite (D1).
7. The move starts empty: no rows or files are copied from Railway.
8. SVG images must keep working.
9. The spike deploys with wrangler, not `cf`.
10. The item Workflow lives in `pipeline/`.
11. The spike finds Workflows' limits (step output size, step count, sleep) itself, rather than through separate research first.
12. Image processing (SVG to PNG, WebP) is a step of the item Workflow. The spike checks whether it can run in TypeScript inside a Worker. If it can't, it runs in a container of its own, separate from the API.
13. The design to pursue is the **Chosen: TypeScript API + item Workflow** drawing. The spike covers only its unknowns.
14. Everything nagara runs on Cloudflare is TypeScript: the API, the item Workflow and the pipeline. `tts/` stays in Python on Modal.
15. Schema migrations are hand-written SQL files applied with wrangler.
16. The Workflow reaches Modal over HTTP, so `tts/` gains two web endpoints, one to start synthesis and one to fetch the result.
17. The API stays a separate deployable in `api/`, outside `pipeline/`.
18. The modules inside `pipeline/` may be reorganized to keep each part separate.
19. The Workflow is flattened. The extraction Workflow's steps become steps of the item Workflow, and DomainQueue serves the item Workflow as a whole.
20. The spike tries reaching Gemini through AI Gateway.
21. The spike uses the real Gemini and Firecrawl keys, and the coordinator asks you when it needs something to test them.

Changes to the unknowns:
- **Unknown 3:** with the Workflow flattened, the open point is how a running item Workflow waits for its domain's lease from DomainQueue and gives it back. Today DomainQueue starts a new Workflow per job instead.
- **Unknown 7:** Gemini through AI Gateway replaces calling Gemini directly from a Worker.
