{"pane_id":"w3W:pF","label":"scout: how tests work","agent":"scout-how-tests-work","status":"done","message":"**Summary:** Both sides test against fakes. Neither has recorded real-service traffic for the extraction Worker, and no test crosses the API/pipeline boundary. The only link is a cassette fabricated by hand to mimic the pipeline's HTTP responses.

## `pipeline/` (about 1060 lines of tests)
- **Runner:** vitest 4.1 with `@cloudflare/vitest-plugin`, the new plugin that replaces `vitest-pool-workers` (`package.json`). Tests run inside workerd/miniflare, using `wrangler.jsonc` and `main: ./src/index.ts` (`vitest.config.ts:4-12`). `pnpm test` builds the injection bundle first.
- **Workflow:**
  - `test/extraction-workflow.test.ts:21-121` has 7 cases. They call `env.EXTRACTION.create(...)` and cover recipe validate, revise, author, not-article, retry exhaustion and a dead dynamic worker.
  - `test/helpers/http.ts:62` and `test/read-path.test.ts:8,34` use `introspectWorkflowInstance(env.EXTRACTION, id)` with `await using`.
- **Durable Objects:**
  - `domain-queue.test.ts` and `job-index.test.ts` use `runInDurableObject`, `runDurableObjectAlarm` and `reset` from `cloudflare:test`.
  - They check queue behaviour through `env.EXTRACTION.get(id)` resolving or rejecting (`domain-queue.test.ts:42,88-89`).
  - `JobIndex` is addressed by name (`job-index.test.ts:7`).
- **Dynamic Workers:** `LOADER` is a real `worker_loaders` binding (`wrangler.jsonc:6`), run locally in miniflare, not faked.
  - `runtime.test.ts`, `runtime-smoke.test.ts` and `dynamic-workers-proof.test.ts:12` call `runRecipe(env, recipe, html)` for real.
  - The CPU-limit kill test is `it.skip` (`dynamic-workers-proof.test.ts:19`) because miniflare doesn't enforce `cpuMs`. It is only checkable on the real edge.
- **Flue agents / AI Gateway / Workers AI:** never called in tests.
  - `src/workflow/world.ts:26` defines a `WORLD_SEAM` global-symbol seam with `runRecipe`, `dispatchAgent` and `readAgent`.
  - `test/helpers/world.ts:11-64` installs a double through it. `worldWithAgents` returns canned author/revision replies, such as `NOT_ARTICLE_REPLY` and `GAVE_UP_REPLY` (`world.ts:15-16`), and can record dispatches. `slowRunWorld` adds delay.
  - `settlement.test.ts` and `prompts.test.ts` test the agent-side parsing and prompts as pure functions.
  - The model is configured as a var, `agentModel: cloudflare-ai-gateway/workers-ai/@cf/zai-org/glm-5.3-flash` (`wrangler.jsonc:22`).
- **Recordings:** none. There is no cassette, no `fetchMock` and no `vi.mock` in `pipeline/test`.
- **Article fixtures:** a single hand-written HTML string plus recipe declarations, in `test/fixtures/article.ts` (`articleHtml`, `passingRecipe`). No real-article files.
- **HTTP surface:** `http.test.ts` and `read-path.test.ts` call `exports.default.fetch(new Request("https://pipeline.test/jobs/..."))` (`helpers/http.ts:17,27`).

## `api/tests/` (pytest, vcrpy via pytest-recording)
- **Record mode:**
  - It is replay-only. CI runs `uv run pytest --block-network` (`.github/workflows/api.yml:30`).
  - Re-record by hand with `--record-mode=rewrite` plus a key in `api/.env` (`test_firecrawl_fetch.py:8-10`).
  - Cassettes are YAML (`version: 1`) in `api/tests/cassettes/<test_module>/<test_name>.yaml`.
- **Config:** `conftest.py:130-160` sets `vcr_config`.
  - It filters the headers `authorization`, `x-api-key`, `x-goog-api-key` and the two `cf-access-client-*` headers.
  - It matches on method, scheme, host, port, `item_normalized_path`, query and `item_normalized_body`.
  - The normalizers (`conftest.py:32-51`) rewrite `itm_<8hex>` to `itm_fixed` so a fabricated cassette replays against any item id.
- **Count and coverage:** 39 cassettes. By request URI there are 33 on `https://extraction.test`, 11 on `https://api.firecrawl.dev` and 5 on `https://generativelanguage.googleapis.com` (Gemini).
  - `extraction.test` is a fake host. The `extraction_service` fixture (`conftest.py:55-63`) points `cloudflare_extraction_url` at it and sets a replay Firecrawl key. Those cassettes are fabricated, not recorded from the Worker.
  - Extraction-Worker cassettes are in `test_extraction_client/` (5), `test_extraction_resolve/` (16), `test_extraction_retry/` (5) and `test_extraction_source/` (5). They show the boundary shapes, for example `POST /jobs` with `{html, job_id, domain, recipe}` returning 201 `{"job_id":..., "state":"queued"}`.
  - Firecrawl is recorded for real in `test_firecrawl_fetch/test_firecrawl_http_surface.yaml`. The other Firecrawl cassettes, which probably sit in the `extraction_source`, `extraction_retry` and `extraction_resolve` folders, are fabricated.
  - Gemini is in `test_describe/` (4) and `test_describe_images/` (1).
- **Modal:** it is mocked, not recorded. `@patch("app.service.tts.modal")` replaces `modal.Cls.from_name...spawn` and `modal.FunctionCall.from_id...get` (`test_tts_client.py:13-51`). `test_extraction_resolve.py:6` says "Modal stays mocked per the suite's habit".
- **Fetch and spawn stubs:** several tests patch `app.service.pipeline.steps.FirecrawlFetcher` and `spawn_extraction` / `resolve_extraction` directly (`conftest.py:121-122`, `test_main.py:88,150,236`).
- **Fixtures:** only images, `tests/fixtures/sample.png` and `bakeoff_realpython.jpg` (`test_describe_images.py:31,35`; `test_image_storage.py:14`). The HTML in API tests is inline strings (`test_main.py:236`).

## Across the boundary
- **Shared fixtures:** none between `pipeline/test/fixtures/article.ts` and `api/tests`.
- **Cross-boundary tests:** none. Each side tests its half of the HTTP contract against its own double of the other.
- **Worth knowing for the TS port:**
  - The `extraction.test` cassettes encode the pipeline's job contract (`POST /jobs`, `GET /jobs/{id}`, states, error strings).
  - The Worker's own job-endpoint tests in `pipeline/test/http.test.ts` and `read-path.test.ts` are the other copy of that contract.
  - Folding extraction into the item Workflow will make both obsolete.

I did not read the `cloudflareTest` plugin's bindings beyond `wrangler.jsonc`. I did not check which of the 11 Firecrawl cassettes are real recordings versus fabricated.","ask":false}

`WORLD_SEAM` is how the extraction Workflow's tests swap out the parts that reach outside the Workflow. Those parts are running a recipe in the sandbox and talking to the Flue agents. It's defined in `pipeline/src/workflow/world.ts`:
- `WorkflowWorld` (lines 11–24) is an interface with three calls: `runRecipe`, `dispatchAgent` and `readAgent`.
- `WORLD_SEAM` (line 26) is a global symbol, `Symbol.for("nagara.workflow.world")`.
- `resolveWorld` (lines 28–39) checks `globalThis` for an object stored under that symbol. If one is there, the Workflow uses it; otherwise it uses the real recipe runtime and agent gateway.
- In tests, `test/helpers/world.ts` stores a stand-in under the symbol. It returns canned agent replies such as "not an article" or "gave up", and can record what was sent. So the Workflow tests never call the model or AI Gateway.

It works through a global rather than an injected argument because the test builds the Workflow instance through its binding, so the test has no way to hand it constructor arguments. In the item Workflow, the same seam could cover Firecrawl, Gemini and Modal: real calls in production, canned responses in tests.

1. `api/` moves to Cloudflare.
2. The database moves to Cloudflare.
3. The file bucket moves to Cloudflare.

13. The design to pursue is the **Chosen: TypeScript API + item Workflow** drawing. The spike covers only its unknowns.
14. Everything nagara runs on Cloudflare is TypeScript: the API, the item Workflow and the pipeline. `tts/` stays in Python on Modal.
15. Schema migrations are hand-written SQL files applied with wrangler.
16. The Workflow reaches Modal over HTTP, so `tts/` gains two web endpoints, one to start synthesis and one to fetch the result.
17. The API stays a separate deployable in `api/`, outside `pipeline/`.

# Cloudflare Workflows: spawn-and-resolve and its limits

verified: 2026-09-13

Answers how to run a long job on Cloudflare Workflows from another service in a spawn-and-resolve shape, what the hard limits are, and which creation semantics are safe to retry. Distilled from a survey run while designing an extraction service against Cloudflare Workflows.

## Knowledge

- Instances get caller-chosen ids: `env.WORKFLOW.create({ id, params })`, ids up to 100 chars matching `^[a-zA-Z0-9_][a-zA-Z0-9-_]*$` (REST also reserves `cf_` + 64 hex). Mapping instances to your own identifiers is a documented use, and `params` is any JSON value.
- `create()` is not idempotent: it throws when the id exists within the retention window (3 days free, 30 paid, configurable per instance). `createBatch()` is idempotent and skips existing ids. Create-or-resume is two operations: create, catch the exists error, then `get(id)`; `get()` throws for an unknown id, so an id that does not resolve yet can mean queued-behind-something rather than absent.
- The finished `run()` return value is fetchable as the instance's `output` through `instance.status()` from a Worker route, or through the REST GET-instance endpoint, which also returns a per-step array with attempts and timings. The status set is queued, running, paused, errored, terminated, complete, waiting, waitingForPause, unknown.
- Wall clock per instance is unlimited. The binding constraint is CPU per step invocation: 10 ms on the free plan, 30 s default and configurable to 5 minutes via `limits.cpu_ms`. Waiting on network I/O does not burn CPU, so a job of many slow model calls fits; a single heavy parse must fit the CPU budget.
- Payloads: params, events and non-stream step results are each capped at 1 MiB. Larger artifacts go to external storage (R2) with a reference passed instead. Whether `run()`'s final output shares the 1 MiB cap is undocumented.
- Steps run once durably via `step.do`; the return value is persisted and replayed on resume instead of re-executing. Branching is plain JS control flow inside `run()`. Steps support per-step retries (limit up to 10,000, fixed or backoff delay) and a per-attempt timeout; `NonRetryableError` stops retrying; `step.sleep` waits up to 365 days; `step.waitForEvent` waits from 1 second to 365 days.
- Concurrency: instances with different ids run concurrently; sleeping or event-waiting instances do not count toward the running cap (50,000 paid, 100 free), so millions can wait at once. Creates are rate-limited per account (300/s paid).
- Conflicting limits exist across Cloudflare's own docs: the Agents SDK page says 10 MB state per workflow and 30 minutes per step; the Workflows reference says 100 MB to 1 GB per instance and unlimited step wall clock. The Workflows reference matches observed behavior reports; treat the Agents SDK table as stale.

## Sources

- Workers API (updated 2026-08-12): https://developers.cloudflare.com/workflows/build/workers-api/
- Limits (updated 2026-06-15): https://developers.cloudflare.com/workflows/reference/limits/
- Trigger Workflows (updated 2026-07-13): https://developers.cloudflare.com/workflows/build/trigger-workflows/
- Sleeping and retrying (updated 2026-07-09): https://developers.cloudflare.com/workflows/build/sleeping-and-retrying/
- REST instances create/get: https://developers.cloudflare.com/api/resources/workflows/subresources/instances/

content.content:
# Cassettes over mocks

The api suite replays a service behind an HTTP boundary, the extraction pipeline, from cassettes exactly as it replays firecrawl and gemini, so the client's real serialization and parsing run against the recorded shapes. Mocks are for calls that are not plain HTTP.

- Record against the real service when it can run: `wrangler dev` needs no account and serves on localhost. The conftest's matching rules carry the hard parts: body matching disambiguates POSTs to one URL, and repeated identical GETs replay in recorded order, which is a poll sequence.
- Fabricate when the service does not exist yet: a cassette is YAML of request and response pairs, hand-built from the boundary contract. The trade is that a recorded cassette is evidence the service answered, and a fabricated one is the contract restated as a fixture, so drift passes unnoticed. Both sides are ours, so the risk is small.
- The unreachable case cannot be a cassette: a refused connection produces no interaction. Point the client at 127.0.0.1, a closed port that refuses instantly, with recording disabled for that one test. The failure is a genuine network one.
- Mocks stay for what is not HTTP: modal's spawn-and-resolve, the gemini describer SDK.
- Volatile ids break replay: minted `itm_` handles differ per run. A registered matcher normalizes them on both sides, cassette and request, so one cassette replays across any mint.

Date: 2026-10-04. Sources are marked (trial), (source) or (docs). I ran no trial of my own. The installed plugin's type declarations (trial-level, read from disk) are the strongest evidence below.

## Package state
- `@cloudflare/vitest-plugin` latest is 1.3.6, published 2026-10-02 (source: registry.npmjs.org). The repo's `pipeline/node_modules` has 1.1.13 installed.
- It is the renamed `@cloudflare/vitest-pool-workers` (renamed in 1.0.0). The old name's last release is 0.22.0, 2026-08-18.
- It is actively maintained: 1.3.x patch releases shipped within the last week (source: CHANGELOG).

## 1. Workflow introspection APIs
- **T1:** Documented and supported.
  - https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/testing/vitest-integration/test-apis/ (page dated 2026-09-28) documents `introspectWorkflow()` and `introspectWorkflowInstance()` with examples (docs).
  - https://developers.cloudflare.com/workflows/build/test-workflows/ ("Test Workflows", updated 2026-04-22) exists. The fetch tool returned no body for it, so I can't say what it says about HTTP mocking (docs, not verified).
  - The repo has a `fixtures/vitest-plugin-examples/workflows` example (source).
- **T2:** Replaces a whole step's result, an error, an event or a sleep. It does not replace an individual HTTP request. All of this is read from the installed 1.1.13 `types/cloudflare-test.d.ts`:
  - `introspectWorkflowInstance(binding, id)` returns:
    - `waitForStepResult({name, index?})`
    - `waitForStatus(status)`
    - `modify(fn)` with `disableSleeps(steps?)`, `mockStepResult`, `mockStepError`, `forceStepTimeout` and `mockEvent`
    - the instance's output and error, read after the instance completes or errors
  - `introspectWorkflow(binding)` applies the same `modify` to every instance created afterwards, for instances whose IDs you don't control. Both support `await using` disposal.
  - A mocked step skips its callback, so any `fetch` inside that step never runs.
  - Steps not mocked run the real code, including any `fetch` in them.
- **T3:** Supported. It is present in the installed 1.1.13 and in the docs dated 2026-09-28.
  - 1.3.0 changelog: `introspectWorkflow*` still need a Workflow binding. Passing a Workflow from `ctx.exports` gives an error explaining how to add one. Instances created through `ctx.exports` are introspected too.

## 2. Outbound fetch mocking
- **T1:**
  - `fetchMock` from `cloudflare:test` was removed in 0.13.0, the release that added Vitest 4 support. The CHANGELOG says: mock `globalThis.fetch` or use ecosystem libraries like "MSW (recommended)" (source).
  - Cloudflare's examples fixture `request-mocking` demonstrates MSW via `setupFiles` (`network.enable()`, `resetHandlers`, `disable`). It has `direct.test.ts`, `exports.test.ts` and `websocket.test.ts`. Last commit 2026-08-19 (source).
  - The docs pages I fetched don't mention `fetchMock`, MSW or `outboundService`: test-apis (2026-09-28), configuration (2026-08-20), known-issues (2026-08-20) and the integration index (2026-08-20). Cloudflare therefore documents no HTTP mocking approach in prose, only in the fixture and changelog.
  - `outboundService` is a Miniflare option. Its type is present in miniflare 5.20260918.0-alpha (source: type declarations). The plugin's 0.20.0 changelog says to use it in place of the removed `miniflare.fetchMock` override. I found no docs page for it in the vitest context.
- **T2:**
  - MSW or a `globalThis.fetch` patch replaces individual HTTP requests, by URL and method.
  - `outboundService` replaces all outbound requests of a worker with a handler worker or function. Per its Miniflare type it can be a service name, `kCurrentWorker` or a function (source).
  - Neither replaces bindings.
  - I did not verify whether MSW or a `globalThis.fetch` patch set in the test file or `setupFiles` intercepts `fetch` calls made inside a Workflow step. The Workflow engine runs in a Durable Object, possibly in a different I/O context. The examples only cover direct `worker.fetch` and `exports.default.fetch` invocation.
- **T3:**
  - `fetchMock` from `cloudflare:test`: removed in 0.13.0 (pool-workers).
  - `miniflare.fetchMock` override option: removed in 0.20.0. Breaking change.
  - MSW: no plugin-side support needed. It is the recommended pattern in the changelog and a fixture in the 1.x examples.
  - `outboundService` (miniflare override): present in the miniflare dependency. Its status as a supported plugin option is not stated anywhere I read.

## 3. Test doubles injected by the code itself
- **T1:** Not documented by Cloudflare as a Workflow-testing method. The changelog's "mock `globalThis.fetch`" for HTTP is the nearest documented analogue. The Cloudflare docs I fetched say nothing about global-symbol seams or env-based injection.
- **T2:**
  - A global-symbol seam, or an env var read by the code, can replace whatever the code routes through it: a whole step's work, a single call or a binding. It decides what is replaced. The cost is that the test hooks live in production code paths.
  - Replacing a binding is native: `miniflare` override options and `wrangler` config in `cloudflareTest({...})` can define test-only bindings (docs, configuration page).
  - Service bindings can point at a test worker, which can act as a stub for an HTTP endpoint (general Miniflare capability, not checked here).
- **T3:** Not applicable. It is a code pattern. It needs nothing from the plugin and cannot be removed by it.

## Cross-cutting
- `modify` helpers run at the step level, so a step that makes three HTTP calls is mocked as one unit.
- Mocked steps and MSW or `outboundService` compose: a mocked step skips its callback, and unmocked steps still make real `fetch` calls unless intercepted.

## Not verified
- The body of the "Test Workflows" page (the fetch returned only its title and date).
- Whether MSW or a `globalThis.fetch` patch intercepts `fetch` inside Workflow steps.
- Whether `outboundService` is accepted through the `cloudflareTest({ miniflare })` override in 1.3.6. I saw only the Miniflare type and the changelog pointer.
- Whether 1.3.6 differs from 1.1.13 in the introspection API. I read 1.1.13's types and the 1.3.0 changelog entry only.","ask":false}

content.text:
The `WORLD_SEAM` approach is not what Cloudflare recommends. Cloudflare documents two other mechanisms, one for each layer, and neither is a global swapped in by the code.

**What Cloudflare documents**

| Mechanism | What it replaces | Status |
|---|---|---|
| **Workflow introspection:** `introspectWorkflow` and `introspectWorkflowInstance`, with `modify` | A whole step: `mockStepResult`, `mockStepError`, `mockEvent`, `disableSleeps`, `forceStepTimeout`. A mocked step never runs its body, so any HTTP request inside it never happens. | Supported. In the Cloudflare docs dated 2026-09-28 and in the plugin version installed in `pipeline/` (1.1.13). The latest plugin is 1.3.6. |
| **MSW** (Mock Service Worker, a library that intercepts HTTP requests) | Individual HTTP requests, by URL and method | It replaces `fetchMock`, which the plugin removed in 0.13.0. The changelog calls MSW "recommended", and Cloudflare's examples include an MSW fixture. The prose docs don't mention it. |
| **A seam in the code** (`WORLD_SEAM`) | Whatever the code sends through it: a call, a whole step's work, a binding | Cloudflare doesn't document this as a way to test Workflows. Its cost is that the test hook sits in production code. |

**Unverified:** whether MSW catches requests made inside a Workflow step. The Workflow runs inside a Durable Object, possibly in a separate request context, and Cloudflare's MSW examples only cover requests made directly from the Worker.

**The project's own wiki goes another way.** The local entry `cassettes-over-mocks` says to replay HTTP boundaries from recordings, so the real request-building and response-parsing code runs. It keeps mocks only for what isn't plain HTTP, which today means the `modal` client and the Gemini SDK. In the new design Firecrawl, Gemini through AI Gateway, and Modal are all plain HTTP from a Worker. By that entry, they'd be replayed rather than replaced through a seam or a mocked step.

**New unknowns from our discussion:** most of what we settled refines unknowns already on the list (2, 3, 5, 7). One is new:
- **9. Testing the item Workflow:**
  - whether step mocking through introspection covers what the tests need
  - whether MSW catches requests made inside a Workflow step
  - which of these, or the seam, the tests use for Firecrawl, Gemini and Modal

Decisions:
1. `api/` moves to Cloudflare.
2. The database moves to Cloudflare.
3. The file bucket moves to Cloudflare.
4. Railway stops being used for nagara.
5. `tts/` stays on Modal.
6. The database switches from Postgres to SQLite (D1).
7. The move starts empty: no rows or files are copied from Railway.
8. SVG images must keep working.
9. The spike deploys with wrangler, not `cf`.
10. The item Workflow lives in `pipeline/`.
11. The spike finds Workflows' limits (step output size, step count, sleep) itself, rather than through separate research first.
12. Image processing (SVG to PNG, WebP) is a step of the item Workflow. The spike checks whether it can run in TypeScript inside a Worker. If it can't, it runs in a container of its own, separate from the API.
13. The design to pursue is the **Chosen: TypeScript API + item Workflow** drawing. The spike covers only its unknowns.
14. Everything nagara runs on Cloudflare is TypeScript: the API, the item Workflow and the pipeline. `tts/` stays in Python on Modal.
15. Schema migrations are hand-written SQL files applied with wrangler.
16. The Workflow reaches Modal over HTTP, so `tts/` gains two web endpoints, one to start synthesis and one to fetch the result.
17. The API stays a separate deployable in `api/`, outside `pipeline/`.
18. Each module inside `pipeline/` is as independent of the others as it can be.
19. The Workflow is flattened. The extraction Workflow's steps become steps of the item Workflow, and DomainQueue serves the item Workflow as a whole.
20. The spike tries reaching Gemini through AI Gateway.
21. The spike uses the real Gemini and Firecrawl keys, and the coordinator asks you when it needs something to test them.
22. The existing Firecrawl cassettes are reused as test data.
23. The spike checks whether the Gemini cassettes still match once requests go through AI Gateway.
24. Whether a test covers the API starting the item Workflow across the two deployables stays open until the spike.
25. The spike doesn't look for a way to record and replay HTTP traffic inside workerd.
26. The spike covers unknowns 1–8.
27. The spike deploys to the real Cloudflare account under spike-only names, uses a separate Modal app, and deletes everything it created when it finishes.

Questions this raises:
- Is unknown 9 in the spike?
- Your "go with the seam if it's the recommended approach" was conditional on something that turned out false. Do the tests use step mocking through introspection, MSW for HTTP, the seam, or a mix?
- Decisions 22 and 25 are in tension: the Firecrawl cassettes are kept as test data, but nothing in workerd will replay them yet. Does unknown 9 also check whether MSW can serve them?

Base directory for this skill: /home/agus/workspace/asermax/claude-plugins/mahou/skills/spike

Load mahou:basics first. Then read `.mahou/spike.md` if present.

# Spike

A spike is code written to answer a question. The answer is the product; the code is not. You build it small, run it against reality, and throw it away. It never merges, never the starting point of the real implementation, which gets built clean once the question is settled.

## The process

1. **Name the question.** One design question that reading and asking cannot settle: whether an approach holds, what shape something should take, what actually happens when the real thing runs. A question a document or a scout can answer does not need a spike.

2. **Build the smallest working version of the real thing.** It works, against real inputs, under real conditions. A mock answers nothing. Build only what the question asks about. Build it in the change's scratch folder, at `spikes/<question-slug>/`, so nothing of it touches a repository.

3. **Run it against reality and observe.** Whatever can tell you the answer is the reactor: real data, a real run, a person reacting, another agent attempting the task. You choose the reactor for the spike; it is not prescribed. What happens is the result, and the gap between that and what was expected is usually the finding.

4. **Iterate in rounds under a strategy.** A round changes something and produces an outcome; the outcome settles a decision or sharpens the question, and the next round builds on what settled. Load the strategy for changing things from `references/strategies/` and pick it per spike:

   | Strategy | When |
   |---|---|
   | [One variable per round](references/strategies/one-variable.md) | The question has a working baseline and the rounds narrow in on failures |
   | [Variants in parallel](references/strategies/variants-in-parallel.md) | Several answers could work and only evidence picks between them |

   A spike may invent its own strategy; when one works, it is a candidate for mahou:learn to add here.

5. **Stop when the question is answered.** Record the answer and the findings in the spike's folder. Every surprise is input to the design that follows. The artifacts stay as reference material for whoever builds the real thing.

## What a spike never does

It never decides for the user. The spike brings the outcome; the design decisions it raises go back as questions. It never grows a second question. A new question is a new spike. Extracting the real thing from spike code keeps every shortcut the throwaway allowed.
